newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF to leave Moscow without agreeing loan payment.
newsitem.headline: IMF to leave Moscow without agreeing loan payment.

text.p: The IMF delivered a stinging rebuke to Russia's economic policymakers on Thursday and its latest monitoring mission will leave Moscow without recommending the release of a tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan.

The Russian Central Bank said in a statement that the IMF was worried about Russia's ability to meet its commitments on revenues and other issues. "The parties failed to reach a common opinion on a number of problems," it said.

The IMF declined to comment on the statement, issued after talks between its delegation and Russian ministers and central bank experts. Russian officials close to the talks had admitted that the discussions were difficult.
"Tax collection is the trickiest problem," one official said.

The Washington-based organisation delayed handing over one tranche of the loan in July and its experts were clearly angered this time that Russia had made little progress in meeting the terms agreed after that delay.
"Differences of opinion emerged over...the realisation of the decisions taken in July-August 1996 and aimed at strengthening budget revenues," the central bank statement said.
The statement capped a month of good and bad news for the Russian economy.

Analysts are cheered at a get-tough policy on tax, a high speculative rating for Russia's planned Eurobond issue and at the abrupt departure of security chief Alexander Lebed, accused by President Boris Yeltsin of blatant presidential ambitions.
But parliament, dominated by communists and their conservative allies, first rejected the 1997 budget and then censured the government for its inability to meet budget plans.
The president of autonomous Tatarstan said on Thursday that Moscow's threats to use bankruptcies in a crusade against tax-dodging firms would not work in his region.

"A feverish struggle for taxes and vain attempts to collect them remind us of the stagnation (of the last years of the communist regime)," said Mintimer Shaimiyev, who has won wide autonomy for his Volga river region.
"Now, as then, they are trying to get more milk from chronically undernourished cows."
Ministers have named Tatarstan's KamAZ truckmaker as one of four big tax debtors and said it was in line for bankruptcy proceedings. Shaimiyev said the firm was not liable for tax.

Russia's huge unpaid tax bills are part of a chronic cycle of non-payments running through the Russian economy, where tax evasion is virtually a national sport. Low tax revenues mean the government cannot afford to pay its bills, which in turn leaves factories unable to find cash to pay workers.

"The crisis in public financing is Russia's next big problem," said Christopher Granville, economist at United City Bank. "Some really hard lessons are going to have to be learned by all concerned, just as they were with stabilisation."
Economists have welcomed the government's tough new approach, which includes the creation of a special tax commission to encourage firms to pay their bills.
"These threats to certain companies are the way forward," said Gavin Rankin of Troika-Dialog.
"The IMF is going to continue (paying) but it is very much a carrot and stick approach. Nothing should be taken for granted and the IMF is not going to be a pushover."
Parliament's objections to the 1997 budget draft centred on overambitious revenue targets and inadequate funding for the military and the social sector.
The government presented a revised draft on Thursday, shaving one trillion roubles off both spending and revenue.
Ministers said spending for industry, the military and the social sphere would rise, but gave no details of where the money would come from.
